title: Pawn storms and opposite-side castling

D0.outcome: Explains that a pawn storm needs pieces massed behind it and a pawn barrier that can be broken, and that with opposite-side castling the game becomes a race.

D1.outcome: Finds the lever that opens a file against the castled king and counts the pieces behind it.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled positions, decides whether to storm, defend or counter, and labels the choice practical or sound.

D3.outcome: Predicts when the storm fails (intact barrier, defender's pieces near) and counts the race.

misconceptions: Pawn moves are free when attacking.
conditions: Many pieces can be massed behind the pawns before the opponent counterattacks the advanced pawns.
With opposite castling, pawns are cheap and open lines are the point; speed decides.
Against a castled king the pawn attack succeeds only if the pawn barrier on the third rank can be broken.
contrasts: The same pawn moves, with the barrier intact and the defender's pieces near.
'the player who attacks first usually wins' is folk wisdom, not a theorem.
